Content:
For a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix differential equation
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),]

Content:
we know that if [MATH: A] has distinct eigenvalues, the general solution is
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.]

Content:
This formula works even when the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1, \lambda_2] are complex. However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome.

Content:
A more direct method is to find just one of the complex solutions, say [MATH: \mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},] and separate it into its real and imaginary parts.

Content:
[MATH: x_{1}(t)|= v_{1}e^{λ_{1}t}; = w_{1}(t)_(⏟)_(Real Part) + \textrm{i}w_{2}(t)_(⏟)_(Imaginary Part)]

Content:
The general real-valued solution is then a linear combination of these two parts:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t)]

Content:
Note: This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only one of the complex solutions, [MATH: \mathbf x_1(t)?]

Content:
The reason is that the second solution, [MATH: \mathbf x_2(t),] doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix [MATH: A,] the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in conjugate pairs, which means [MATH: \mathbf x_2(t)] is simply the complex conjugate of [MATH: \mathbf x_1(t).]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),] it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of [MATH: \mathbf x_1(t).]

Content:
To build our general solution, we just need two linearly independent real solutions. The key facts are the following:

Content:
- For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part [MATH: \mathbf w_1(t)] and the imaginary part [MATH: \mathbf w_2(t)] are always linearly independent.
- Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution.

Content:
So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with [MATH: \mathbf x_2(t)] at all.
